title: Exit signs and emergency lights: safe teardown
summary: Most commercial buildings have emergency lights and exit signs. Each holds a rechargeable battery (NiCd, sealed lead-acid or, on newer units, lithium), LED or halogen lamp heads and a charger board that switches to battery when the power fails. They are wired to 120 V, 277 V or 347 V and mounted high: switch off, prove the wires dead, then unplug the battery before anything else.

steps.text: First look for a permanent label saying the sign contains tritium, or a sign with no wires and no battery that glows by itself: it is self-luminous, not electric, so stop and leave it whole (see the notes). Otherwise, find the breaker that feeds the unit. Switch it off and lock it, or tape a note over it, then switch off every other source that could feed the building: a generator, a solar or battery inverter, a UPS or a central battery system. The lamps should now come on from the battery: that is normal. If they stay dark, the battery may be flat, or the unit may be fed from another circuit or source: treat it as live until you have proved it dead.
steps.warn: These units are wired to 120 V, 277 V or 347 V circuits. A dead grid is no proof: a generator, solar or battery inverter or UPS may still feed the building. Switch those off too and tag them.

steps.text: Stand a ladder on firm, level floor with a helper footing it, clear of doors and walkways. If you have one, use a wooden or fibreglass ladder, not a metal one, near wiring. Wear safety glasses and light the work area. Keep your meter and tools in a pouch, not in your hands, and don't work alone. Plan to hand the unit down in pieces, not carry it down.
steps.warn: Keep three points of contact on the ladder. Never lean out sideways to reach the unit; move the ladder.

steps.text: Open the housing. Plastic units: press the two snaps at the bottom, swing the housing up and pull it off its mounting plate. Exit signs: pop the snap-fit face or cover. Steel units: undo the screws on the front panel or open its hinged cover. Don't touch any wire or terminal yet.

Prove the supply dead before you touch anything inside, using a meter rated for at least 600 V. With a meter you have just checked on a known live source, measure at the unit's mains leads or input connector: live to neutral, live to earth and neutral to earth (see safety_mains_isolation). Then check the meter on the live source again.
steps.warn: If anything reads more than a few volts AC, stop. Find the right breaker before you touch the wires.

steps.text: Take off rings and watch. Unplug the battery connector. On slip-on terminals, pull the negative (black, minus) one off first and tape it at once, then the positive (red, plus) and tape it. The lamps go out.
steps.warn: The battery keeps the lamps and charger board live with the breaker off, and halogen heads get hot while lit. A 12 V lead-acid battery can burn a hand or melt a tool if a terminal or bare connector touches steel or a tool.

steps.text: Unscrew the mounting plate (or the steel unit) from the junction box and ease it forward on its leads, with the helper taking its weight; don't pull on the wires and don't touch bare conductors. The building wires, joined to the unit's leads with wire connectors, are now in view. Before you disconnect them, prove them dead again where you will touch them: with the meter you proved on a known live source, measure live to neutral, live to earth and neutral to earth on bare conductor or terminal metal that shows (don't force probes into wire connectors), then prove the meter on the live source again. If anything reads more than a few volts, or you can't reach any metal, stop and find the right breaker or source.
Undo the wire joints joining the unit's leads to the building wires. Cap and tape each building wire on its own, then push them back into the junction box.

Hand the unit down to your helper, who takes its weight before you let go. On a steel unit with a lead-acid battery, unstrap the battery first (terminals taped) and hand it down on its own, then the cabinet.
steps.warn: Steel units with lead-acid batteries are heavier than they look; some ship at about 11 kg. Never hold one with both hands on a ladder: hand the battery and the cabinet down separately.

steps.text: On the bench, release the strap, clip or bracket and lift out the battery. Note its type, volts and capacity from its label.
steps.warn: Swollen lithium: see safety_swollen_lithium. Cracked, leaking or crusted lead-acid packs: gloves, glasses, keep upright (see safety_lead_acid). Leaking NiCd cells hold caustic electrolyte and cadmium: gloves and glasses, rinse skin and eyes with plenty of water, no baking soda.

steps.text: Tape over the battery terminals or plug, or put the battery in its own plastic bag, so nothing can short it.

Take out the charger board: on many plastic units, flex the snap at each end and slide it straight out; on others undo its screws. Do this first: photograph its leads, drain any large capacitor on the board with the resistor tool and check it with the meter (see safety_discharge_capacitor), and only then unplug the leads.

Take off the lamp lenses by easing them over their snaps with your thumbs; prying under them with a tool can crack them. Unplug or cut the lamp head leads, leaving long tails, and unscrew the heads if you want them.
Test the battery before you trust it: see Testing below. Batteries in these units are often years old.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The battery.** The most useful part. Three kinds turn up:
  - **Nickel-cadmium (NiCd) packs.** Small LED twin-head units use 3.6 V packs, three 1.2 V cells (Lithonia ELM2 LED; Sure-Lites APEL). LED exit signs may have a 1.2 V NiCd battery, with a typical life of 7 to 9 years (Lithonia LQM). Good for small LED lights, torches and radios that run on 3 to 4 cells. Cadmium can harm health and the environment if the cells are mishandled, and EPA says rechargeable batteries don't go in the trash (EPA batteries). Don't open, crush or burn them: a fire gives off toxic fumes, and the contents of a leaking cell are corrosive (Motorola NiCd SDS).
  - **Sealed lead-calcium (lead-acid) blocks.** Steel units hold 6 V or 12 V batteries rated 27 to 100 W for 90 minutes, with a typical life of 3 to 5 years (Lithonia ELTC). Good for small 6 V or 12 V lighting and radio setups. Handle them as safety_lead_acid says and test them with test_lead_acid.
  - **Lithium iron phosphate.** Some newer units use 9.6 V or 12.8 V lithium packs (Lithonia ELM4L-ELM6L). Treat them like any lithium battery: never puncture, bend or short them, and store them on a non-flammable surface.
- **Lamp heads.** LED heads on small units run at 3.6 V, about 0.8 to 1.5 W each (Sure-Lites APEL; Lithonia ELM2 LED). Newer heads reach 5.3 W (Lithonia ELM4L-ELM6L). Steel units often have metal heads with 12 W PAR36 halogen lamps (Lithonia ELTC). Run a halogen head straight from a battery of its label voltage; it doesn't care which way round. Try an LED head on a current-limited supply at its label voltage before you wire it to a battery, since it may rely on the charger board to limit its current.
- **Charger board.** A current-limited charger with an automatic switch to battery when mains fails, a cut-off that stops the battery running too flat, and a test switch (Lithonia ELM2 LED; Sure-Lites APEL). Kept together with its battery and heads, the whole unit is an automatic light that comes on when the power fails, wherever you have a mains circuit, for example one fed by a generator. Refit it the way it came off: a hard-wired mains connection, made with the circuit proved dead.
- **Indicator LEDs, test switch and wire.** Small spares.

## Variations

- **Shape.** Exit signs with a lit face; plastic twin-head units; and steel cabinets with two metal heads. The steel ones usually hold the biggest batteries.
- **Supply voltage.** The same unit can take 120 V, 277 V or, in Canada, 347 V, chosen by which lead is connected (Lithonia ELM install). Assume 277 V or 347 V in commercial buildings until you know.
- **Opening.** Many plastic units are snap-fit with no screws (Sure-Lites APEL; Lithonia LQM). The Lithonia ELM opens by pressing two snaps at the bottom and swinging the housing up (Lithonia ELM install). Steel units use screws.
- **Battery connection.** A single plug on many plastic units (Lithonia ELM install), slip-on spade terminals on steel units (Lithonia ELTC), and polarised terminals on others (Sure-Lites APEL).
- **Flat batteries.** The low-voltage cut-off disconnects the lamps before the battery is ruined; on one unit it trips at 80% of rated voltage (Sure-Lites APEL). So a unit found dark after a long outage may still have a usable battery: charge it and test it. A battery left on a charger board with no mains for a long time can be damaged (Lithonia ELM install).
- **Line latch.** A unit that has never had mains since installation may not light when power fails (Sure-Lites APEL).
- **Working at height.** Near live wiring, OSHA wants ladders with nonconductive side rails, the area around the ladder kept clear, and nothing carried that could throw you off balance (OSHA ladders).

## What to leave

- **Dead batteries.** Keep them out of fires and water. Tape the terminals and store them for a recycler (EPA batteries).
- **Exit sign faces and plastic housings**, unless you want small boxes or plastic sheet.
- **Self-test and radio boards** on newer units: of little use without the rest of the system.
- **Self-luminous tritium signs.** A sign with no wires and no battery, with a permanent label saying it contains tritium, is not electric. EPA says an intact one emits no radiation, but a damaged one can release tritium: leave it whole, and if one is broken leave the area (EPA tritium exit signs).

## Testing what you got out

- **NiCd pack.** Rest it a few hours and measure. A healthy pack reads roughly its label voltage (1.2 V a cell). If you have mains, charge it in its own unit for a full day (the Lithonia ELM's maker allows 48 hours for a full charge), then run it on its own lamp heads and time how long they stay bright (Lithonia ELM install). The units are rated for 90 minutes when new.
- **Lead-acid block.** Follow test_lead_acid. A 6 V block is three cells, so read its numbers as half a 12 V battery.
- **LED heads.** Power them from a battery of their label voltage through a small resistor or a current-limited supply first, to check them before you build them in.
